title: Seasons by Latitude: How the Year Tilts
description: See how seasons change with latitude with Seasons by Latitude — solstices, equinoxes, day length and why the tropics barely notice. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, on June 21 New York gets 15.1 hours of daylight while London gets 16.6 and the equator gets its usual twelve — same day, three different planets of light.
quick_answer: Seasons by Latitude shows how the seasons play out at your latitude — day lengths at the solstices and equinoxes, and when your hemisphere leans toward the Sun. Pick a latitude and read the year's shape: fierce high up, gentle in the tropics, flipped down south.

Moving from Miami to Minneapolis (or Manchester)? Your December daylight is about to change character — preview it here.
Day length drives plants as much as temperature does; latitude sets the calendar both follow.
Southern-hemisphere trips invert everything: Sydney's Christmas is high summer, a fact this page makes mechanical rather than surprising.
Day length on the June solstice (computed): equator 12.0 h, New York 15.1 h, London 16.6 h, Tromsø 24 h. Latitude is the volume knob on the seasons.
Around March 20 and September 22, every latitude gets ~12 hours — computed New York: 12.1 h on March 20. The equinoxes are the year's two fair days.

faq: Earth's axis tilts 23.44° and keeps pointing the same way as we orbit, so each hemisphere takes its turn leaning sunward. Distance to the Sun is not the cause — Earth is nearest the Sun in early January.
Mild ones: day length and noon sun vary little inside the tropics, so seasons there are usually described as wet and dry instead of hot and cold.
The same tilt, seen from the other hemisphere: December leans the south sunward. Their summer solstice is the north's winter one.
Nearly — refraction and the Sun's size stretch the day slightly past 12 hours (New York computes to 12.1 h on March 20). The name promises equal night; geometry adds a tip.
How extreme can day length get?
From the equator's fixed ~12 h to the poles' single six-month day and night — the checker on this site tests any latitude's extremes.
Slowly: the tilt itself wobbles between ~22.1° and 24.5° over ~41,000 years, which is why the tropics and circles creep (currently ~15 m a year).

Astronomers date from solstices/equinoxes; meteorologists use whole calendar months for statistics. Your forecast's 'first day of winter' (Dec 1) and the solstice (Dec 21) are both right, differently.
It sets the Sun's angle and day length — the energy budget. Oceans, altitude and winds then argue with it, which is why London out-warms its latitude.
